---
title: "Diagnostic test accuracy meta-analysis"
subtitle: "Sensitivity, specificity, summary point and diagnostic odds ratio"
---

Use this module when each study gives a 2x2 accuracy table: true positives,
false positives, false negatives and true negatives. Follow [the three-step
flow](flow.qmd), but step 2 is much shorter and step 3 is the most different of
all the modules.

## Step 1, the data

| Column | What it is |
|---|---|
| `study` | the study label |
| `TP` | true positives |
| `FP` | false positives |
| `FN` | false negatives |
| `TN` | true negatives |

In the comparative module there is one more column, `test`, with the name of the
test, and each study appears twice, one row per test.

Extra columns, such as `Region`, stay available for subgroup analysis. The
**Data check** verifies the required ones, counts the studies and flags negative
or blank cells.

## Why this module is different

In diagnostic meta-analysis the outcome is **bivariate**: sensitivity and
specificity move together and are correlated. A more sensitive test is usually
less specific, because the threshold moves. That is why the model is the
bivariate binomial GLMM, and not two separate models. That is the model the
Cochrane Handbook for DTA Reviews v2.0 specifies in chapter 10.

This has a practical consequence: looking at pooled sensitivity alone gets you
nowhere. The main result is the **operating point**, sensitivity and specificity
together, with their confidence intervals.

## Step 2, the parameters

This is the shortest step 2 in MetaVidence, because most of the choices in a
bivariate model are not configurable field by field.

### Single test module

**Outcome name** goes into titles and file names.

**Analysis model** (default `Random-effects`) affects the sensitivity,
specificity and diagnostic odds ratio forest plots.

::: {.callout-note}
## The bivariate model ignores this field
The Reitsma bivariate model is always random-effects, by construction. Switching
to `Fixed-effect` changes the forest plots, but neither the summary point nor the
summary operating point.
:::

There is no `sm`, `Method`, `Tau method`, prediction interval or group name
here: none of those fields applies to the bivariate model.

### Comparative module

Besides **Outcome name**, there are **Test A** and **Test B**, which fill
themselves with the names found in the `test` column. They define which test is
compared against which, and the order the two appear in the figures.

## Step 3, export and results

### Single test

**Sensitivity forest plot** and **Specificity forest plot**, one for each, with
sensitivity computed as TP / (TP + FN) and specificity as TN / (TN + FP).

**Summary point**, with the studies, the pooled sensitivity and specificity, a
95% confidence region and a 95% prediction region. There is no curve and no
AUC: those belong to the HSROC model, which the handbook notes cannot be fitted
in R with lme4. The bivariate model estimates a point, so a point is what the
plot shows.

::: {.callout-important}
## The forest plots show studies, not a pooled estimate
The forests deliberately carry no pooled diamond. Averaging sensitivity and
specificity separately ignores the correlation between them, which is what
section 10.2.3 of the handbook rules out. Every pooled number in this module
comes from the bivariate fit, and there is only one of each.
:::

**Diagnostic odds ratio**, with its own forest plot. The DOR summarizes accuracy
in a single number, combining sensitivity and specificity. It is useful for
comparing tests, but it says nothing about where the balance between the two
errors lies, so it does not replace the sensitivity and specificity pair.

**Threshold effect**, the correlation between sensitivity and the false-positive
rate across studies, with the Deeks test for small-study effects. A positive
correlation suggests the studies used different positivity thresholds, which is
the confounder specific to diagnostic accuracy.

::: {.callout-note}
## There is no subgroup analysis here
To the bivariate model a subgroup and a head-to-head test comparison are the
same thing: a covariate. The handbook says so plainly, calling them both
"group". That model lives in the comparative workflow, so splitting one test by
a column belongs there rather than being duplicated as a weaker version here.

The app warns when there are fewer than 4 studies: the bivariate model estimates
5 parameters and converges anyway, but the estimate becomes unstable.
Converging is not the same as being trustworthy.
:::

### Comparative

**Sensitivity by test** and **Specificity by test**, the forest plots split by
test.

**Comparative summary points**, both tests on the same plot, each with its own
confidence region. Both come from one joint model, grouped by study, so a
paired design keeps its pairing.

**Overall comparison**, **Sensitivity comparison** and **Specificity
comparison**: three likelihood-ratio tests, one for overall accuracy and one for
each component. Having the overall test significant and the two specific ones
not significant is common and informative: the tests differ in the balance
between the two errors, not in either one alone.

::: {.callout-important}
## The comparative module requires paired studies
Each study must have assessed both tests in the same population. Studies with
only one of the tests stay out of the joint comparison. Comparing tests assessed
in different populations means comparing populations, not tests.
:::
